bio.line1: I’m a Product Designer working on B2B digital products. I shape end-to-end flows, draw the interfaces, and build the design systems that keep them coherent over time.
bio.line2: Before designing, I wrote code — Angular, TypeScript, Sass — in real production teams. That part of the past isn’t a second job offer; it’s a quiet superpower: I design with implementation in mind, document like a developer reads, and stay close to engineering without losing the product point of view.
bio.line3: Behavioral Design certified, fluent in French, English and Spanish. Based in Saint-Malo since 2023, after a decade of motion and editorial work in Madrid.
bio.line4: I like quiet interfaces, opinionated documentation, and the moment a developer says “ah, that’s clear.”

hero.title: Design <it>System.</it>
hero.sub: Building the design system and the UI foundations of a B2B HR platform — from a single accent color to twenty-five components, three teams, and one shared vocabulary with engineering.

kit.label: Reviews table
kit.caption: One component, built from the tokens
kit.aria: A reviews data table — one component assembled from the Staff & Go design system, with participants, status chips and dates.

context.title: A young product,
context.left: Staff & Go is a French B2B platform for human-resources operations: annual reviews, contracts, payslips, leaves, onboarding — across dozens of establishments per client. When I joined, the product had grown faster than its UI: dozens of screens, every button slightly different, every developer choosing their own paddings.
context.rightTop: The brief, eventually, became simple: make the product feel like one product. Build a design system from scratch. Document it for developers and project managers. Keep designing new features in parallel.
context.rightBottom: I worked alongside the engineering team in Angular 16. Not as a developer — as a designer who reads code, opens a PR when a class name is wrong, and writes documentation a developer can copy-paste from.

approach.title: Tokens first,
approach.left: I started from the bottom: design tokens. Colors, spacing, radii, type, motion. Named them so a developer would name them the same way. Mapped each one to a Sass variable.
approach.rightTop: Only then I drew components — and only the ones the product actually used. Each component shipped with anatomy, variants, behaviors, usage rules, edge cases, and a short note on how to implement it. The Figma file and the Angular code shared the same vocabulary.
approach.rightBottom: The point was never to win a Figma file. It was to make every product decision faster than the previous one.

engineering.title: I don't hand off —
engineering.left: My background in front-end means I review implementations against Figma, open the right files, and propose corrections in a vocabulary the team trusts.
engineering.rightTop: This isn't about being a designer-developer. It's about removing friction: when a component drifts, I notice; when documentation is unclear, I rewrite it; when a token gets named twice, I catch it before review. The product moves forward faster, with fewer surprises.

outcomes.title: One product,
outcomes.left: After eighteen months, every product screen used the same components. Onboarding a new developer took half the time. New features could be drawn and built in days, not weeks.
outcomes.rightTop: Confidential business numbers stay confidential — but the artifacts and reasoning are available on request. Reach out if you'd like a walkthrough.

documentation.title: A system you can read,
documentation.left: A component isn't done when it's drawn — it's done when a developer or PM can use it without asking me. So every component shipped with its own page: an intro on what it's for, its states and variants, the rules for which to use when, do's and don'ts, and the exact tokens and specs to implement it.
documentation.rightTop: Each page started from the same question: how will this be misused? The do/don't pairs answered it before code review did — and everything was indexed, so the team could self-serve instead of pinging me.
documentation.rightBottom: Written so a developer could copy-paste the spec and a PM could follow the decision.

docPlate.introBody: The button's types, sizes and colours cover the combinations a view needs — keeping visual hierarchy and a consistent experience. Icons and colour make each action understandable and accessible.
docPlate.doText: One primary action per view — the decisive next step.
docPlate.dontText: Two primaries competing — the user can't tell what matters.

hawi.subtitle: A mobile app to reduce loneliness in older adults. From discovery workshops to a role-based interactive Figma prototype.
hawi.heroVisualAlt: Illustration of a family embracing while looking at the Hawi app on a phone

ohana.label: Ohana /oˈhana/
ohana.body: n. Hawaiian. The circle of people who are your family — whether by blood, choice, or time.

context.title: A concept for
context.left: Hawi started as a graduation brief: design a mobile app that addresses loneliness in older adults. Not a medical tool, not a panic button — a presence layer for families and the people around them.
context.rightTop: The name comes from Hawaiian. Hawi is a place — a small, remote town. We kept it as a reminder: the people we are designing for are often at a distance, even when they live nearby.
context.rightBottom: Role: UX/UI designer. Timeline: six months from first workshop to interactive prototype. Tools: Figma, paper, a lot of sticky notes.

research.title: Talking to the circle,
research.left: Discovery ran in Madrid with three groups: older adults aged 68–82, their primary family carers, and care-home coordinators — through co-design workshops and in-depth interviews.
research.rightTop: The pattern was consistent: older adults didn't feel lonely — the people around them felt powerless. The anxiety of not knowing, not reaching, not being present was the real problem to solve.

design.title: Three roles,
design.left: The core design decision: three separate views of the same data. The elder gets simplicity. The family carer gets reassurance and coordination. The coordinator gets an overview without intrusion.
design.rightTop: Every screen passed through paper sketch, blockframe, and hi-fi wireframe before the prototype. The Locator screen — where is Dad — was the hardest to get right.

ohanaFlow.title: Concept
ohanaFlow.desc: A family app for older adults — designed for the people around them.

ohanaFlow.title: Discovery
ohanaFlow.desc: Co-design workshops and interviews with families and care professionals in Madrid.

ohanaFlow.title: Design
ohanaFlow.desc: Role-based flows: the elder, the family carer, the coordinator. Three views, one data model.

ohanaFlow.title: Prototype
ohanaFlow.desc: Interactive Figma prototype, presented in ES / EN / FR to clients and stakeholders.

actors.name: The elder
actors.body: Lives alone, uses a phone with help. The interface is stripped back: large targets, one main action per screen, nothing that feels like surveillance.

actors.name: The family carer
actors.body: An adult child managing care from a distance. Needs reassurance and coordination — to know, to reach, to act — without living inside the app.

actors.name: The coordinator
actors.body: A care-home professional overseeing several residents. Needs an overview and task control, not intimacy.

actors.name: The ohana
actors.body: Neighbours and friends. Occasional presence, low-friction touchpoints — the wider circle the concept is named after.

boceto.heading: Locator — first sketch
boceto.deviceLabel: Paper sketch of the Locator screen
boceto.desc: Hand-drawn after the first discovery session. The Locator is the family carer's anchor: where is Dad, is he reachable, what can I do right now?

blockframe.heading: Structure before noise
blockframe.desc: Blocks only — no colour, no copy. Testing the hierarchy: header status, map zone, action strip. One question per block.

wireframe.heading: Closest to final
wireframe.desc: Brand tokens applied. Real copy tested at size. Route and call are separated by visual weight, not just position.
wireframe.deviceLabel: Hi-fi wireframe of the Locator screen

mockup.body: The chat screen is the heart of Hawi. Not a messaging app — a presence layer. Read receipts, voice notes, quick reactions. Designed for one-handed use and low visual acuity.

gazella.subtitle: A women's health app that tunes training and nutrition to the menstrual cycle. I led two new areas: an editable cycle calendar and the premium nutrition section.
gazella.heroVisualAlt: Gazella home screen with the day's training and cycle-based articles

insight.label: The premise
insight.body: Bodies aren't clockwork. The app planned everything from one date entered at sign-up — and never let you change it. But cycles shift: different day, different length, some months none at all.

context.title: Joining a product
context.left: Gazella is a health app for women that adapts running, training and nutrition to the phases of the menstrual cycle. I joined an existing product as its sole UX/UI designer, under a creative director, to lead two new areas.
context.rightTop: The app already had a brand and a working engine. What it lacked was control: the cycle — the thing the whole product is built on — was a single fixed input.
context.rightBottom: Role: sole UX/UI designer. Studio: Akimad. Both areas shipped as a first version, built to iterate.

calendar.title: A cycle you can
calendar.left: The original app asked for your last period once, at sign-up, and calculated every workout from it. There was no way to change it. So the moment a cycle ran short, late or skipped, the plan drifted from the body it was meant to follow.
calendar.rightTop: The calendar gave that control back. A direct entry in the bottom nav, period start and end set by tapping the days, the current phase shown in context, and training days marked with dots — recalculated whenever the dates change.
calendar.rightBottom: I benchmarked nearly every cycle-tracking app on the market, then prioritised the smallest set of features that made the calendar trustworthy enough to ship and iterate.

nutrition.title: Designing the first
nutrition.left: Nutrition was a client mandate: the startup's first attempt at revenue. The brief was a premium tier — recipes adapted to each cycle phase, locked behind a subscription. I designed the UI and the upgrade flow.
nutrition.rightTop: To stop premium feeling like a wall, I studied how other apps structured recipe content and shopping lists, then gave the paid section a distinct look — so it read as better and different, not just blocked.
nutrition.rightBottom: I was honest about the risk: with countless dedicated nutrition apps out there, I doubted users would pay for it. I said so. The call was the client's — designing it well was mine.

callout.heading: A shopping list that writes itself.
callout.body: The piece I pushed for: generate the shopping list straight from a recipe's ingredients. Want to cook it? The items are already there — no copying by hand. A small, daily kind of useful that gives a premium tier a reason to exist.

recipe.cap: Recipe detail — ingredients, steps, macro breakdown
recipe.alt: Full Gazella recipe screen for a poke bowl

nutShots.emptyAlt: Empty state of the shopping list

reflection.title: What I'd keep,
reflection.left: Two lessons stuck. Design for the real body, not the ideal one — the editable cycle mattered precisely because nothing is regular. And design within a startup's real limits: ship a first version that's honest about being one.
reflection.rightTop: I'd still question the premium bet. Charging for nutrition in a crowded market was a leap of faith more than a validated need. Voicing that — and designing it as well as it could be anyway — is the part I'm proud of.

fiche.subtitle: Redesigning the densest screen in a B2B workforce-management app — the employee record — from an overwhelming wall of fields into something legible and learnable.

heroDiagram.caption: A wall of fields → sections
heroDiagram.aria: Diagram: an undifferentiated wall of equal fields on the left becomes a record organised into labelled sections on the right.

insight.label: The premise
insight.body: The whole app was hard to learn. A dense management tool with a steep curve. I took on one of its most overloaded areas — the employee record — with a pattern meant to scale beyond it.

context.title: A powerful tool,
context.left: Staff & Go is a B2B workforce-management platform — payroll, leave, HR, scheduling. Powerful, but dense: across the whole product, new users faced a steep learning curve. The employee record was its most overloaded screen.
context.rightTop: Every detail of a worker lived there — identity, contracts, social security, banking, documents — crammed into tight forms in small type, spread across views that were hard to find.
context.rightBottom: Role: Product Designer, working alongside the PMs and the head of development to keep friction low for users and feasible for engineering.

problem.title: Density,
problem.left: Too much information, too small, too hard to scan. Finding the right view took effort; the screen punished newcomers. The goal wasn't more features — it was less cognitive load.
problem.rightTop: Before touching pixels I benchmarked comparable tools and gathered design references, then mapped what the record actually needed to show, and in what order.

redesign.title: Structure
redesign.left: The fix was architecture, not paint. I grouped the record into clear, labelled sections with breathing room and a predictable order, so the eye always knows where to look. Same data, far less effort to read.
redesign.rightTop: I designed the real states too — accounts initialised, activated, deactivated, not yet set up — so the screen stayed coherent across every case, not just the happy path.
redesign.rightBottom: And I designed it with engineering in the room, so the structure was something the team could actually build and ship incrementally.

ba.beforeNote: Dense form, small type, hard to scan
ba.beforeAlt: Original employee record — dense form layout (anonymised)

mobile.heading: One order, learned once.
mobile.body: On every breakpoint the record reads as the same ordered sections — Profile, Identification, Birth, Contact, and so on. The employee and establishment records share that order, so a professional user learns the pattern once and reuses it everywhere.
mobile.alt: Redesigned employee record on mobile, scrollable (anonymised)

outcome.title: Shipped in phases,
outcome.left: The redesign rolled out in phases — deliberately, to ease users into the change rather than relabel everything overnight. The ordered-section pattern was made to extend from the employee record to establishments and beyond.
outcome.rightTop: A reminder that in a dense B2B tool the highest-impact design move is often not adding — it's making what's already there legible, consistent, and kind to a first-time user.
